## Appendix E Maximal Margin of $S_{n,k}$ in dimension $O(k\log n)$ from Compressed Sensing

We begin by defining the restricted isometry property.

#### Definition 2 ([15]).

Let $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ be a matrix. For $1\leq k\leq n$ and $\delta_{k}\in(0,1)$ we say that $M$ satisfies $(\delta_{k},k)$ restricted isometry property (RIP) if for any vector $v$ that is at most $k$ -sparse,

$$ \|v\|_{2}^{2}(1-\delta_{k})\leq\|Mv\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|v\|_{2}^{2}(1+\delta_{k}). $$

#### Remark 1.

If $M$ satisfies $(\delta_{k},k)$ -RIP, it also satisfies $(\delta_{m},m)$ -RIP for any $m\leq k,\delta_{m}\geq\delta_{k}.$

We now state a theorem of [15] in the language of our work.

#### Theorem E.1 (Modification of [15]).

Suppose that the matrix $V=(V_{1}V_{2}\cdots V_{n})$ satisfies $(\delta_{3k},3k)$ -RIP such that $\delta_{3k}\leq 1/3.$ Let $c$ be a vector with support $T$ of size at most $k.$ Then, there exists a real vector $U_{j}$ such that:

- 1. $\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle=c_{j}$ whenever $i\in T.$

- 2. $|\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle|\leq\frac{\delta_{3k}}{(1-2\delta_{3k})\sqrt{|T|}}\|c\|_{2}$ whenever $i\not\in T.$

- 3. $\|U_{j}\|_{2}\leq C(\delta_{3k})$ for some constant $C$ that depends only on $\delta_{3k}.$

#### Proof.

Parts 1 and 2 appear directly in [15, Lemma 2.2] except that we have replaced orthogonality $\theta$ values by RIP $\delta$ values using [15, Lemma 1.2] and used the fact that $V$ also satisfies $(\delta_{3k},k)$ -RIP and $(\delta_{3k},2k)$ -RIP as in the above remark.

Part 3 follows from the following fact (in the notation of [15], $U_{j}=w$ ).

$$ \|U_{j}\|_{2}=\|w\|_{2}=\|\sum_{i=1}^{+\infty}(-1)^{i-1}w_{i}\|_{2}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{+\infty}\|w_{i}\|_{2}\leq K(\delta_{3k})\sum_{i=1}^{+\infty}\Big(\frac{\delta_{3k}}{1-\delta_{3k}}\Big)^{i-1}\leq 2K(\delta_{3k}), $$

where all inequalities but the last are in [15, Lemma 2.2]. The last follows from $3\delta_{3k}\leq 1.$ ∎

Now, to apply this theorem, we need a matrix satisfying strong RIP-properties. It turns out that this is achieved by random Gaussian matrices.

#### Proposition 3.

[[15, 8]] Suppose that $d\geq Ck\log(n/k)$ for some sufficiently large constant $C$ and let $\delta=1/6.$ Then, with high probability, the matrix $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}$ in which each entry is independent $\mathcal{N}(0,1/d)$ satisfies $(1/6,3k)$ -RIP.

#### Proof.

The proof follows directly from [15, Lemma 3.1] by choosing the right parameters. Namely, $S=3k,$ $m=n,$ $p=Ck\log(n/k).$ Then, $r=S/m=3k/n.$ Hence, for the binary entropy function $H,$

$$ \displaystyle f(r)=\sqrt{n/(Ck\log n)}(\sqrt{3k/n}+\sqrt{2H(3k/n)}) \displaystyle=O\Bigg(\sqrt{n/(Ck\log(n/k))}\sqrt{3k/n}\sqrt{\log(n/3k)}\Bigg)=O(C^{-1/2}). $$

Therefore, for some large enough $C,$ it holds that $f(r)\leq 1/128.$ By [15, Lemma 3.1] with $\epsilon=1,$

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}[1+\delta_{3k}\geq(1+2f(r))^{2}]\leq 2\exp(-mH(r)/2) \displaystyle=2\exp(-n\Theta(k\log(n/k)/n))=2\exp(-\Theta(k\log(n/k))). $$

Altogether, with high probability $1-\exp(-\Omega(k\log(n/k))),$ $\delta_{3k}\leq(1+1/64)^{2}-1\leq 1/6.$ ∎

#### Corollary 4.

For some large enough $C,$ there exists a margin $\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$ -embedding of $S_{n,k}$ in dimension $Ck\log(n/k).$

#### Proof.

The proof follows immediately by Theorem E.1 and Proposition 3. Namely, let $\widetilde{V}=(\widetilde{V_{1}},\widetilde{V_{2}},\ldots,\widetilde{V_{n}})$ be a random Gaussian matrix of size $d\times n$ with $d=Ck\log(n/k).$ With high probability, the following two properties hold: $\widetilde{V}$ satisfies $(1/6,3k)$ -RIP and each column of $\widetilde{V}$ has norm at most $2$ (apply the RIP with $v=e_{i}$ ).

As $\widetilde{V}$ satisfies the $(1/6,3k)$ -RIP, then we know there exists $\{\widetilde{U}_{j}\}^{N}_{j=1}$ such that $\langle\widetilde{U_{j}},\widetilde{V_{i}}\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}$ if $A_{ji}=1$ and $|\langle\widetilde{U_{j}},\widetilde{V_{i}}\rangle|\leq\frac{1}{4\sqrt{k}}$ if $A_{ji}=0.$ This follows by setting $c$ to be the vector $c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}A_{j,:}$ in Theorem E.1.

Now, let $\bar{V_{i}}=(\widetilde{V_{i}},(5/8)^{1/2}k^{-1/4}))$ and $\bar{U_{j}}=(\widetilde{U_{j}},-(5/8)^{1/2}k^{-1/4}).$ We can easily check that $\langle\bar{U_{j}},\bar{V_{i}}\rangle\geq\frac{3}{8\sqrt{k}}$ if $A_{ji}=1$ and $\langle\bar{U_{j}},\bar{V_{i}}\rangle\leq-\frac{3}{8\sqrt{k}}$ if $A_{ji}=0.$ Finally, we know that $\|\bar{V_{i}}\|_{2}\leq 2,\|\bar{U_{j}}\|_{2}\leq C(1/6)=O(1).$ Thus, setting $V_{i}=\frac{\bar{V_{i}}}{\|\bar{V_{i}}\|_{2}}$ and $U_{j}=\frac{\bar{U_{j}}}{\|\bar{U_{j}}\|_{2}},$ we obtain $\langle{U_{j}},{V_{i}}\rangle\geq\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$ if $A_{ji}=1$ and $\langle{U_{j}},{V_{i}}\rangle\leq-\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$ if $A_{ji}=0.$ ∎

#### Remark 2.

We note that Corollary 4 falls short of our main results Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.6 in two ways. First, it only provides margin $\Omega(1/\sqrt{k})$ instead of the optimal $(1+o_{k}(1))/(2\sqrt{k}).$ It might be possible to fix this by more carefully keeping track of the constants. The biggest challenge seems to be the norm of $C(\delta)$ from Theorem E.1.

Much more important, however, seems the limitation that in the $k$ -sparse setting, only results for margin $\Theta(1/\sqrt{k})$ seem possible from Theorem E.1. Concretely, note that if $c$ is unit norm in Theorem E.1 (which is without loss of generality as the inequalities are homogeneous in $(U,c)$ ), there exists some $V_{i}$ such that $\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\leq 1/\sqrt{k}.$ Yet, in the current form of the theorem, it might be the case that $\|U_{j}\|_{2}\times\|V_{i}\|_{2}\geq 1$ as evidenced by the case $V=I$ when $U_{j}=c_{j}.$ Thus, $U_{j}$ needs to be unit norm. Altogether, $\langle\frac{U_{j}}{\|U_{j}\|_{2}},\frac{V_{i}}{\|V_{i}\|_{2}}\rangle\leq 1/\sqrt{k}.$

To compare, our Theorem 1.4 applies also to $k$ -sparse $A$ when a larger margin is possible, say $m=1/k^{1/4}.$ In that case, it will give dimension $O(k^{1/2}\log n).$

At the same time, our Theorem 1.6 gives constructions of smaller margin, say $1/n$ but also in much smaller dimensions. Concretely, $d=\Theta(k^{2})$ for margin $1/n.$

## Appendix F Adapting Theorem 1.5 to general $k$ -sparse matrices

We note that the same proof method of Theorem 1.5 can be applied to an arbitrary relevance matrix. We first need a modified version of Lemma 3. Towards this end, we need the following definition. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a family of subsets of $[n].$ We say that $B\subseteq[n]$ is shattered if for any $C\subseteq B,$ there exists some $S\in\mathcal{S}$ such that $S\cap B=C.$

#### Lemma 5.

Let $A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times n}$ , and let $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be a margin- $m$ embedding of $A$ . Define the linear map $V:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}$ by $Ve_{i}=V_{i}$ . Suppose that $S\subseteq[n]$ is shattered by the family of row supports

$$ \mathcal{C}_{A}\coloneqq\bigl\{\{i\in[n]:A_{ji}=1\}:j\in[N]\bigr\}. $$

Then for any $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ supported on $S$ , it holds that $\|Vx\|_{2}\geq m\|x\|_{1}$ .

#### Proof.

By homogeneity, it is enough to prove the claim when $\|x\|_{1}=1$ . Since $S$ is shattered, there exists some $j\in[N]$ such that for every $i\in S$ , $A_{ji}=1\iff x_{i}>0$ . Therefore,

$$ \left\langle U_{j},\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}V_{i}\right\rangle=\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\geq m\sum_{i\in S}|x_{i}|=m. $$

Indeed, if $x_{i}>0$ , then $A_{ji}=1$ , so $\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\geq m$ , while if $x_{i}<0$ , then $A_{ji}=0$ , so $\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\leq-m$ , and hence again $x_{i}\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\geq m|x_{i}|$ . Since $\|U_{j}\|_{2}=1$ , it follows that

$$ \|Vx\|_{2}=\Big\|\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}V_{i}\Big\|_{2}\geq\Big\langle U_{j},\sum_{i\in S}x_{i}V_{i}\Big\rangle\geq m.\qed $$

Then we can use a nearly identical proof as in Theorem 1.5.

#### Theorem F.1 (Lower bound for $k$ -sparse matrices).

Let $A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times n}$ be such that every row of $A$ has exactly $k$ ones, and let

$$ \mathcal{C}_{A}\coloneqq\bigl\{\{i\in[n]:A_{ji}=1\}:j\in[N]\bigr\}\subseteq 2^{[n]} $$

denote the family of row supports. Suppose $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}$ form a margin- $m$ embedding of $A$ with $m>0$ . Fix $\alpha\in(0,1/2]$ and set $s=\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor$ . If $s\geq 1$ , then

$$ d\geq\frac{\log|\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)|}{\log\!\left(1+\frac{2}{m\sqrt{s}}\right)}, $$

where $\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)\subseteq\binom{[n]}{s}$ is a family such that for all distinct $T,T^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)$ , $|T\cap T^{\prime}|<\frac{s}{2}$ and $T\cup T^{\prime}$ is shattered by $\mathcal{C}_{A}$ .

#### Proof of Theorem F.1.

Let $V$ be as in Lemma 5. Set $s=\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor$ . By definition, there exists a family $\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)\subseteq\binom{[n]}{s}$ such that for any distinct $T,T^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)$ , we have $|T\cap T^{\prime}|<\frac{s}{2}$ and $T\cup T^{\prime}$ is shattered by $\mathcal{C}_{A}$ .

For each $T\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)$ , define the sign vector $\sigma^{T}\in\{\pm 1\}^{T}$ so that $\left\|\sum_{i\in T}\sigma_{i}^{T}V_{i}\right\|_{2}$ is minimized, and set $y_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in T}\sigma_{i}^{T}V_{i}$ .

To bound $\|y_{T}\|_{2}$ , let $\epsilon$ be uniformly random in $\{\pm 1\}^{T}$ . Then

$$ \mathbb{E}\left\|\sum_{i\in T}\epsilon_{i}V_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in T}\|V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,\ell\in T\\
i\neq\ell\end{subarray}}\epsilon_{i}\epsilon_{\ell}\langle V_{i},V_{\ell}\rangle\right]=\sum_{i\in T}\|V_{i}\|_{2}^{2}=s, $$

since the cross terms vanish in expectation. Because $\sigma^{T}$ minimizes the norm, it follows that

$$ \|y_{T}\|_{2}^{2}=\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in T}\sigma_{i}^{T}V_{i}\Bigr\|_{2}^{2}\leq s. $$

Hence $y_{T}\in B_{d}(0,\sqrt{s})$ for all $T\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)$ .

Now define $x_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in T}\sigma_{i}^{T}e_{i}$ so that $Vx_{T}=y_{T}$ . Consider distinct $T,T^{\prime}\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)$ . Since $\operatorname{supp}(x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}})\subseteq T\cup T^{\prime}$ and $T\cup T^{\prime}$ is shattered by $\mathcal{C}_{A}$ , Lemma 5 gives

$$ \|V(x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}})\|_{2}\geq m\|x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}}\|_{1}. $$

Moreover, since every coordinate of $x_{T}$ and $x_{T^{\prime}}$ lies in $\{0,\pm 1\}$ ,

$$ \|x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}}\|_{1}\geq|T\triangle T^{\prime}|=|T|+|T^{\prime}|-2|T\cap T^{\prime}|>2s-s=s. $$

Therefore,

$$ \|y_{T}-y_{T^{\prime}}\|_{2}=\|Vx_{T}-Vx_{T^{\prime}}\|_{2}=\|V(x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}})\|_{2}\geq m\|x_{T}-x_{T^{\prime}}\|_{1}\geq ms. $$

Thus, the vectors $\{y_{T}\}_{T\in\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)}$ are pairwise $ms$ -separated in the ball $B_{d}(0,\sqrt{s})$ . When we rescale by $\tilde{y}_{T}\coloneqq y_{T}/\sqrt{s}$ , we obtain a collection of points in $B_{d}(0,1)$ that are pairwise $m\sqrt{s}$ -separated. By the standard volume bound (for example [66, Corollary 4.2.11]),

$$ |\mathcal{F}_{s}(A)|\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{m\sqrt{s}}\right)^{d}. $$

So, it immediately follows that when $s=\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor$ , we have

$$ d\geq\frac{\log|\mathcal{F}_{\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor}(A)|}{\log\left(1+\frac{2}{m\sqrt{\lfloor\alpha k\rfloor}}\right)} $$

which concludes the proof. ∎

## Appendix G Proofs of Propositions on Margin Importance

#### Proposition 4 (Compositional Generalization and Margin).

Suppose $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ form a margin- $m$ embedding in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ of $S_{n,k}$ with $0<m<1$ . Then for all $T\subset[n]$ with $k\leq|T|\leq\min(k+\frac{2km}{1-m},n-1)$ , there exists an $h\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $i\in T,$ it holds that $\langle h,V_{i}\rangle\geq c$ while for all $j\not\in T,$ $\langle h,V_{j}\rangle\leq c.$

#### Proof of Proposition 4.

For a set $S\subseteq[n]$ with $|S|=k$ , let $U_{S}$ denote the vector such that $\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\geq m$ for all $i\in S$ and $\langle U_{S},V_{j}\rangle\leq-m$ for all $j\notin S$ . Define

$$ h_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ |S|=k}U_{S}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\in S,\ |S|=k}U_{S}+\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\notin S,\ |S|=k}U_{S},V_{i}\right\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\in S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle+\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\notin S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle. $$

Notice that if $i\in S$ , then by definition $\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\geq m$ . If $i\notin S$ , then since $U_{S}$ and $V_{i}$ have unit norm, we have $\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\geq-1$ .

Now fix any $i\in T$ . Then there are exactly $\binom{|T|-1}{k-1}$ sets of size $k$ containing $i$ and contained in $T$ . Also, there are exactly $\binom{|T|}{k}-\binom{|T|-1}{k-1}$ sets of size $k$ contained in $T$ that do not contain $i$ .

So it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\in S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle+\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ i\notin S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle \displaystyle\geq m\binom{|T|-1}{k-1}+(-1)\left(\binom{|T|}{k}-\binom{|T|-1}{k-1}\right) \displaystyle=(1+m)\binom{|T|-1}{k-1}-\binom{|T|}{k} \displaystyle=\frac{(1+m)k}{|T|}\binom{|T|}{k}-\binom{|T|}{k} \displaystyle=\frac{(1+m)k-|T|}{|T|}\binom{|T|}{k}. $$

Furthermore, if $i\notin T$ , then $\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\leq-m$ for all $S\subseteq T$ with $|S|=k$ . Since there are $\binom{|T|}{k}$ subsets of size $k$ contained in $T$ , we get

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle=\sum_{S\subseteq T,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\leq-m\binom{|T|}{k}. $$

We also know that, since $m<1$ ,

$$ \displaystyle k+\frac{2km}{1-m}\geq|T| \displaystyle\implies(1-m)k+2mk\geq|T|(1-m) \displaystyle\implies(1+m)k-|T|\geq-m|T| \displaystyle\implies\frac{(1+m)k-|T|}{|T|}\geq-m. $$

Therefore, for every $i\in T$ and $j\notin T$ , we have

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle\geq\frac{(1+m)k-|T|}{|T|}\binom{|T|}{k}\geq-m\binom{|T|}{k}\geq\langle h_{T},V_{j}\rangle. $$

Therefore, there exists a real constant $c^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfying

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle\geq c^{\prime}\geq\langle h_{T},V_{j}\rangle\qquad\text{for all }i\in T\text{ and }j\notin T. $$

Notice that $\|h_{T}\|\neq 0$ because, since $|T|<n$ , for some $i\notin T$ we have $\langle V_{i},h_{T}\rangle\leq-m\binom{|T|}{k}<0$ . So, if we set $h\coloneqq h_{T}/\|h_{T}\|$ , it follows that there exists an $h\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and $c=c^{\prime}/\|h_{T}\|\in\mathbb{R}$ such that

$$ \langle h,V_{i}\rangle\geq c\qquad\forall i\in T,\quad\text{and}\quad\langle h,V_{j}\rangle\leq c\qquad\forall j\notin T.\qed $$

We note that even a small margin already suffices to force downward generalization. Indeed, once $m\geq\frac{k-1}{2n-k-1}$ , the following proposition implies that every nonempty subset with $1\leq|T|\leq k$ is retrievable. This is related to the notion of a $k$ -neighborly polytope [32]: if $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ forms a $k$ -neighborly polytope, then every subset of at most $k$ vertices forms a face and is therefore exposed by a supporting hyperplane. Thus, every such subset can be separated from the remaining vertices and hence can be retrieved.

#### Proposition 5 (Downward Generalization and Margin).

Suppose $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ form a margin- $m$ embedding in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ of $S_{n,k}$ with $0<m<1$ . Then for all $T\subset[n]$ with $\max\{1,k-\frac{2m(n-k)}{1-m}\}\leq|T|\leq k$ , there exists an $h\in\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}$ such that for all $i\in T,$ it holds that $\langle h,V_{i}\rangle\geq c$ while for all $j\not\in T,$ $\langle h,V_{j}\rangle\leq c.$

#### Proof of Proposition 5.

The case $|T|=k$ is immediate by taking $h=U_{T}$ and $c=0$ , so assume $|T|<k$ .

We use the same notation as in the proof of Proposition 4. Define

$$ h_{T}\coloneqq\sum_{S\supset T,\ |S|=k}U_{S}. $$

Then

$$ \displaystyle\langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle \displaystyle=\left\langle\sum_{S\supset T,\ i\in S,\ |S|=k}U_{S}+\sum_{S\supset T,\ i\notin S,\ |S|=k}U_{S},V_{i}\right\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{S\supset T,\ i\in S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle+\sum_{S\supset T,\ i\notin S,\ |S|=k}\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle. $$

Again, if $i\in S$ , then by definition $\langle U_{S},V_{i}\rangle\geq m$ .

Now fix any $i\in T$ . Then there are exactly $\binom{n-|T|}{k-|T|}$ sets of size $k$ containing $T$ , and so

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle\geq m\binom{n-|T|}{k-|T|}. $$

For $j\notin T$ , the number of sets of size $k$ containing $T$ and $j$ is $\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}$ , while the number of sets of size $k$ containing $T$ but not $j$ is $\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|}$ . Hence, using $\langle U_{S},V_{j}\rangle\leq 1$ when $j\in S$ and $\langle U_{S},V_{j}\rangle\leq-m$ when $j\notin S$ , we have

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{j}\rangle\leq\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}-m\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|}. $$

Thus it suffices to show

$$ \binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}-m\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|}\leq m\binom{n-|T|}{k-|T|}. $$

Since

$$ \binom{n-|T|}{k-|T|}=\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}+\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|}, $$

this inequality is equivalent to

$$ m\geq\frac{\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}}{\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|-1}+2\binom{n-|T|-1}{k-|T|}}=\frac{k-|T|}{k-|T|+2(n-k)}\iff|T|\geq k-\frac{2m(n-k)}{1-m}. $$

Therefore, for every $i\in T$ and $j\notin T$ ,

$$ \langle h_{T},V_{i}\rangle\geq c^{\prime}\coloneqq m\binom{n-|T|}{k-|T|}\geq\langle h_{T},V_{j}\rangle. $$

Since $c^{\prime}>0$ , we have $h_{T}\neq 0$ . Taking $h=\frac{h_{T}}{\|h_{T}\|}$ and $c=\frac{c^{\prime}}{\|h_{T}\|}$ completes the proof. ∎

#### Proposition 6 (Robustness and Margin).

Suppose that the object space $\mathcal{O}$ and the query space $\mathcal{Q}$ are metric spaces with metrics $d_{\mathcal{O}}$ and $d_{\mathcal{Q}},$ respectively. Suppose that the corresponding encoders $f_{\theta}$ and $g_{\phi}$ have relative-bias- $\tau$ and margin $m$ on the datasets $\{Q_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}\subset\mathcal{Q}$ and $\{O_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset\mathcal{O}$ with relevance matrix $A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times n}$ . If $f_{\theta}$ and $g_{\phi}$ are both $L$ -Lipschitz for some $L>0$ , then for every $j\in[N]$ , every perturbation $Q_{j}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Q}$ satisfying $d_{\mathcal{Q}}(Q_{j}^{\prime},Q_{j})<\frac{m}{L}$ preserves perfect retrieval. Namely, $\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle>\tau\quad\text{ if }A_{ji}=1$ and $\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle<\tau\quad\text{if }A_{ji}=0.$ Likewise, the same holds for small perturbations of the objects.

#### Proof of Proposition 6.

Since $d_{\mathcal{Q}}(Q_{j}^{\prime},Q_{j})<\frac{m}{L}$ and $g_{\phi}$ is $L$ -Lipschitz, we have

$$ \|g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime})-g_{\phi}(Q_{j})\|\leq L\,d_{\mathcal{Q}}(Q_{j}^{\prime},Q_{j})<m. $$

Now fix $i\in[n]$ . If $A_{ji}=1$ , then since $f_{\theta}(O_{i})$ has norm $1$ , we have

$$ \bigl|\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime})-g_{\phi}(Q_{j}),\,f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle\bigr|\leq\|g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime})-g_{\phi}(Q_{j})\|\,\|f_{\theta}(O_{i})\|<m. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle \displaystyle=\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime})-g_{\phi}(Q_{j}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle+\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle \displaystyle>-m+(\tau+m)=\tau. $$

Similarly, if $A_{ji}=0$ , then

$$ \displaystyle\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle \displaystyle=\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}^{\prime})-g_{\phi}(Q_{j}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle+\langle g_{\phi}(Q_{j}),f_{\theta}(O_{i})\rangle \displaystyle<m+(\tau-m)=\tau.\qed $$

#### Proposition 7 (Maximal-Margin Embeddings and Sigmoid Loss).

Consider the sigmoid loss with inverse-temperature $t>0$ and bias $b$ over embeddings $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}:$

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};t,b)\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[N],i\in[n]}\log\Big(1+\exp\big((-1)^{A_{ji}}(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)\big)\Big). $$

Then

- 1. If $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};t,b)<\log 2,$ then there exists $m>0$ such that $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is a margin- $m,$ relative-bias- $\frac{b}{t}$ embedding of $A$ .

- 2. If $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ and $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ form a margin- $m_{*}$ , relative-bias- $\tau$ embedding of $A$ where

$$ m_{*}\coloneqq\min\left\{\min_{A_{ji}=1}\left(\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-\tau\right),\min_{A_{ji}=0}\bigl(\tau-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\bigr)\right\}>0. $$

Then

$$ \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)=-m_{*}. $$

#### Proof of Proposition 7.

We begin with part (1). Suppose that $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};t,b)<\log 2$ . For each fixed pair $(j,i)$ , the term $\log\Big(1+\exp\big((-1)^{A_{ji}}(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)\big)\Big)$ is nonnegative. So, it follows that for every fixed pair $(j,i),$

$$ \log\Bigl(1+\exp\bigl((-1)^{A_{ji}}(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)\bigr)\Bigr)<\log 2. $$

Since the function $x\mapsto\log(1+e^{x})$ is strictly increasing, we obtain

$$ (-1)^{A_{ji}}(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)<0. $$

If $A_{ji}=1$ , then $-(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)<0$ , so $t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b>0.$ If $A_{ji}=0$ , then $t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b<0.$

Since there are finitely many pairs, set

$$ m\coloneqq\min\left\{\min_{A_{ji}=1}\left(\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-\frac{b}{t}\right),\min_{A_{ji}=0}\left(\frac{b}{t}-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle\right)\right\}>0. $$

Then $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ form a margin- $m$ , relative-bias- $\frac{b}{t}$ embedding of $A$ .

We now prove part 2. For each pair $(j,i)\in[N]\times[n]$ , define

$$ \gamma_{ji}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-\tau,&A_{ji}=1,\\[4.0pt]
\tau-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle,&A_{ji}=0.\end{cases} $$

Then $\gamma_{ji}>0$ for all $(j,i)$ , and by definition $m_{*}=\min_{j,i}\gamma_{ji}$ .

If $A_{ji}=1$ , then

$$ (-1)^{A_{ji}}\bigl(T\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-T\tau\bigr)=-\bigl(T\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-T\tau\bigr)=-T(\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-\tau)=-T\gamma_{ji}. $$

If $A_{ji}=0$ , then

$$ (-1)^{A_{ji}}\bigl(T\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-T\tau\bigr)=T\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-T\tau=-T(\tau-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle)=-T\gamma_{ji}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)=\sum_{j\in[N],\,i\in[n]}\log\!\bigl(1+e^{-T\gamma_{ji}}\bigr). $$

Since $\gamma_{ji}\geq m_{*}$ for all $(i,j)$ , we obtain the upper bound

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)\leq Nn\log(1+e^{-Tm_{*}})\leq Nne^{-Tm_{*}}, $$

where we used $\log(1+x)\leq x$ for all $x\geq 0$ . For the lower bound, choose $(j_{0},i_{0})$ such that $\gamma_{j_{0}i_{0}}=m_{*}$ . Then $\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)\geq\log(1+e^{-Tm_{*}})$ . Also, for $x\in[0,1]$ , $\log(1+x)\geq\frac{x}{2}$ . Hence for all sufficiently large $T$ (so that $e^{-Tm_{*}}\leq 1$ ), $\log(1+e^{-Tm_{*}})\geq\frac{1}{2}e^{-Tm_{*}}$ . Thus for all sufficiently large $T$ ,

$$ \frac{1}{2}e^{-Tm_{*}}\leq\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)\leq Nne^{-Tm_{*}}. $$

Taking logarithms gives

$$ -Tm_{*}-\log 2\leq\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)\leq-Tm_{*}+\log(Nn). $$

Dividing by $T$ and letting $T\to\infty$ , we conclude that

$$ \lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T,T\tau)=-m_{*}\qed $$

#### Proposition 8 (Large Margins and Quantization).

Suppose that $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , $\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is a margin- $m$ embedding of $A$ . Then there exists a codebook $\mathcal{C}\subset\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$ with size $|\mathcal{C}|\leq\left(1+\frac{8}{m}\right)^{d}$ such that the quantized embeddings $\tilde{U}_{j}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\|x-U_{j}\|$ and $\tilde{V}_{i}\in\arg\min_{x\in\mathcal{C}}\|x-V_{i}\|$ form a margin- $\frac{m}{2}$ embedding.

#### Proof.

There exists a $\frac{m}{4}$ -net $\mathcal{C}$ of size $|\mathcal{C}|\leq\left(1+\frac{2}{\frac{m}{4}}\right)^{d}=\left(1+\frac{8}{m}\right)^{d}$ [66, Corollary 4.2.11]. For any $j\in[N]$ and $i\in[n]$ , we have

$$ |\langle\tilde{U}_{j},\tilde{V}_{i}\rangle-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle|=|\langle\tilde{U}_{j}-U_{j},\tilde{V}_{i}\rangle+\langle U_{j},\tilde{V}_{i}-V_{i}\rangle| $$

Since $\|\tilde{V}_{i}\|=\|U_{j}\|=1$ , we know that $|\langle\tilde{U}_{j},\tilde{V}_{i}\rangle-\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle|\leq\frac{m}{2}$ because $\|\tilde{U}_{j}-U_{j}\|,\|\tilde{V}_{i}-V_{i}\|\leq\frac{m}{4}$ . Therefore, the vectors $\{\tilde{U}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}$ , $\{\tilde{V}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ form a margin- $\frac{m}{2}$ embedding of $A.$ ∎

## Appendix H InfoNCE and Sigmoid in The Free Embedding Model

### H.1 InfoNCE loss

Recall from Proposition 7 that the global minimizers of the following sigmoid loss

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{sigmoid}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};t,b)\coloneqq\sum_{j\in[N],i\in[n]}\log\Big(1+\exp\big((-1)^{A_{ji}}(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle-b)\big)\Big). $$

are exactly the embeddings of $A$ as in Definition 1.

The InfoNCE, on the other hand, defined as

$$ \mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};t)\coloneqq-\sum_{(j,i)\in[N]\times[n]\;:\;A_{ji}=1}\log\Big(\frac{\exp(t\langle U_{j},V_{i}\rangle)}{\sum_{\ell}\exp(t\langle U_{j},V_{\ell}\rangle)}\Big). $$

When $A=I,$ the recent work [7] shows that the global minimizers of InfoNCE have a similar geometry to Definition 1, except that there is a different relative bias $\tau_{j}$ corresponding to each query. Again, they show that the loss converges to 0 as $T\longrightarrow+\infty.$

We note, however, that when $A$ has rows of sparsity more than 1, the loss cannot converge to 0. In fact, for some embeddings of $A$ satisfying the conditions in Definition 1, it is possible that $\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}$ diverges as $T\longrightarrow+\infty.$

#### Proposition 9.

Suppose that $A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times n}$ is such that $A_{ji_{1}}=A_{ji_{2}}=1$ and $\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}$ is an embedding of $A$ such that $\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle\neq\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle.$ Then, $\lim_{T\longrightarrow+\infty}\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T)=+\infty.$

#### Proof.

First note that each summand in (5) is non-negative. Thus,

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T) \displaystyle\geq\log\Big(\frac{\sum_{\ell}\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{\ell}\rangle)}{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle)}\Big)+\log\Big(\frac{\sum_{\ell}\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{\ell}\rangle)}{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle)}\Big) \displaystyle\geq\log\frac{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle)+\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle)}{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle)}+\log\frac{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle)+\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle)}{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle)} \displaystyle\geq\log\frac{\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle)+\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle)}{\min(\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle),\exp(T\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle))} \displaystyle=\log\bigg(1+\exp\Big(T|\langle U_{j},V_{i_{1}}\rangle-\langle U_{j},V_{i_{2}}\rangle|\Big)\bigg) $$

Taking $T\longrightarrow+\infty$ shows that $\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}(\{U_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N},\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};T)\longrightarrow+\infty.$ ∎
